title: Catalysts
hook: The waiting-list card shrank when Laura changed the route between students, not the number of tutors.
counterintuition: More fuel can make a slow path more expensive. A catalyst helps by changing the route, so existing energy reaches the result with less waste.
tryThisNow: Pick one stalled process and ask what would change the path, not add labor. Place one routing aid where the next handoff begins.
keyTakeaway: Catalysts improve reaction rate by changing the path of progress; look for accelerators that help work move faster and cleaner without being used up.

breakdown.fastRead:
Laura's tutor roster looked ordinary until she put it beside the question bank. Students were not waiting because tutors were lazy. They were waiting because every request took the long path through one coordinator.

She matched common questions to peer tutors, left the roster visible, and let students enter the right path without asking permission each time.

A catalyst accelerates a reaction by changing the pathway. It is not extra fuel. It is the thing that lets existing energy move with less waste.
breakdown.deepRead:
"The build is slow again," Luke said while the deploy badge stayed gray. The team could add another server, ask developers to wait, or keep apologizing after every release. Then the cache report showed the same packages being rebuilt from scratch every time.

Catalysts speed reactions without being consumed, and the practical lesson stays inside that support: look for an accelerator that changes the pathway and improves reaction rate without becoming the fuel. Luke's cache did not write code. It did not replace developers. It let the build avoid repeating a costly route, so the same work reached the deploy badge faster and cleaner. A true catalyst changes the way progress travels.

The accelerator is not the hero. The pathway is.

Nicolas found the same pattern after a hospital intake delay. Families waited for language access while nurses called the same interpreter line again and again. The language roster, attached to the family intake form, changed the path. Nurses could see the right interpreter option before the call slip became urgent. No one consumed the roster. It simply helped each case move sooner.

The limit is false labeling. A charismatic helper is not a catalyst unless the process runs differently because of that help. If the person must push every step forever, they are fuel. If a tool, roster, template, or connection changes the route so the system moves without constant rescue, you may have found a catalyst.
breakdown.fullRead:
The repair cafe opened with volunteers standing beside full tool bins and broken appliances that still had no owner. Anke watched a toaster, a lamp, and a sewing machine sit untouched because nobody knew which volunteer should inspect which item first. The room had energy. It lacked a pathway.

That distinction matters because busy rooms often hide slow reactions. People mistake motion for progress, then add more volunteers, more reminders, or more meetings. A catalyst asks for a different diagnosis. If the same handoff wastes effort each time, the next useful move may be a small routing aid, not a bigger crowd.

A catalyst does not solve the whole problem by force. It lowers waste in the route. Anke's repair ticket did that. Each appliance tag named the fault, the tool bin, and the next volunteer. The ticket was not consumed by the repair. It kept guiding the work as the appliance moved from intake to diagnosis to bench.

Where is progress taking the long way because the path is unclear?

That question protects the model from becoming a compliment. Calling someone a catalyst sounds generous, but generosity is not the test. The test is whether the reaction rate changes because the pathway changed. A speaker brief at a conference can be a catalyst if it keeps every presenter from hunting through separate travel notes, greenroom schedules, and slide deadlines. A tutor roster can be a catalyst if it lets students find the right help without waiting for one overloaded coordinator.

You feel the difference when the accelerator stays useful without being used up. Hiroshi at the speaker liaison desk did not personally brief each presenter for an hour. He created one speaker brief that gathered the travel note, greenroom schedule, and AV check into a single path. Presenters still had to prepare. The brief simply helped preparation move cleanly.

Chiara saw the same risk from the opposite side in the bakery. A living starter jar can begin a new loaf, but the handoff was failing because the feeding chart lived in memory. The bench timer, chart, and labeled jar changed the path for the new baker. Without that pathway, Chiara herself had to supervise every feeding. With it, the routine accelerated without requiring her to be the fuel every morning.

Catalysts can be misused. Speed is not automatically wisdom. A routing aid can accelerate the wrong request, a template can speed sloppy work, and a social connector can spread confusion faster than clarity. The model asks for cleaner progress, not merely faster motion. It also asks whether the aid remains available after one pass through the work. The repair ticket still helps after the toaster leaves the bench. The speaker brief still helps after the first presenter reads it. The labeled starter jar still helps on the next shift. That durability is part of the test.

Look for the repeated drag. Find the moment where effort leaves the main path and wanders. Then add the smallest aid that changes the route for the next person through. It should make the system faster without making itself the whole source of energy.

examples.title: Laura Routes the Questions

planSpec.audience: readers who face peer tutor matching network decisions where catalyst is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Laura adds the tutor roster that changes the path, times the question bank, and proves through the waiting-list card that progress accelerated without adding more fuel. Domain: peer tutor matching network.

examples.scenario: The tutor roster curls under Laura's elbow while the waiting-list card grows by six names and the coordinator answers the same algebra request for the third time. The question bank shows that half the students need the same two explanations, but every request still waits in one inbox. Laura must decide whether to recruit more tutors first or route common questions to peer tutors so the coordinator stops being the only pathway.
examples.whatToDo: Match common question types to available peer tutors and put the roster beside the signup form. Let requests enter the right lane immediately.
examples.whyItMatters: The roster does not do the tutoring. It changes the route, allowing existing tutor energy to move faster through the waiting list.

examples.title: Luke Reads the Cache Report

planSpec.audience: readers who face DevOps build cache decisions where catalyst is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Luke adds the cache report that changes the path, times the build timer, and proves through the deploy badge that progress accelerated without adding more fuel. Domain: DevOps build cache.

examples.scenario: "Another server might fix it," Luke says as the build timer climbs past twenty minutes and the deploy badge stays gray. The cache report reveals the same packages rebuilding every release, even when the code change touches none of them. He has to choose between buying capacity or changing the path so completed work is reused before the deploy badge can turn green.
examples.whatToDo: Add the build cache where the pipeline repeats work and track the timer before adding servers. Remove the needless route through old work.
examples.whyItMatters: More servers add fuel. A cache changes the pathway, so the same developer work reaches deployment with less repeated effort.

examples.title: Nicolas Pins the Language Roster

planSpec.audience: readers who face hospital interpreter roster decisions where catalyst is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Nicolas adds the language roster that changes the path, times the family intake form, and proves through the call slip that progress accelerated without adding more fuel. Domain: hospital interpreter roster.

examples.scenario: The intake desk at 7:12 a.m. has three family forms, two call slips, and no clear language path while a nurse waits on the same general phone line. In the postmortem, Nicolas sees that nurses were not refusing help. They were calling the same line for every language. He pins a roster to the intake form so the next family enters the right channel sooner.
examples.whatToDo: Put the interpreter roster at intake and connect each language to the right contact path. Make access faster without asking nurses to improvise.
examples.whyItMatters: The roster is not consumed by any one case. It speeds each case by changing the route from request to interpreter.

examples.title: Anke Tags the Appliances

planSpec.audience: readers who face community repair cafe queue decisions where catalyst is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: volunteers standing idle with broken appliances
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anke adds the repair ticket that changes the path, times the tool bin, and proves through the appliance tag that progress accelerated without adding more fuel. Domain: community repair cafe queue.

examples.scenario: At 9:30 a.m., Anke sees a toaster beside the tool bin, a lamp on the floor, and three volunteers waiting for direction. The appliance tag says only "broken," so each helper has to rediscover the fault. Before the queue grows, she has to decide whether to add another volunteer or create a repair ticket that sends each item to the right bench with the right tool.
examples.whatToDo: Add a ticket that names the fault, tool bin, and next bench. Route each appliance instead of relying on volunteers to guess.
examples.whyItMatters: The ticket accelerates repair without doing the repair. It changes how work moves through the room.

examples.title: Hiroshi Builds the Brief

planSpec.audience: readers who face conference speaker liaison desk decisions where catalyst is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hiroshi adds the speaker brief that changes the path, times the greenroom schedule, and proves through the travel note that progress accelerated without adding more fuel. Domain: conference speaker liaison desk.

examples.scenario: You are at the speaker liaison desk with a greenroom schedule, three travel notes, and a presenter asking where to upload slides ten minutes before rehearsal. Hiroshi sees the same question coming from the next presenter in line. He must decide whether to answer each question by hand or build one speaker brief that puts prep details in the order presenters need them.
examples.whatToDo: Create the brief around the presenter path: travel note, greenroom time, AV check, slide upload. Use it before answering one-off questions.
examples.whyItMatters: A liaison can become fuel by answering forever. A brief becomes catalytic when it lets many speakers move cleanly without fresh rescue.

examples.title: Chiara Labels the Starter Jar

planSpec.audience: readers who face bakery starter handoff decisions where catalyst is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: new baker losing the living starter
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chiara adds the starter jar that changes the path, times the feeding chart, and proves through the bench timer that progress accelerated without adding more fuel. Domain: bakery starter handoff.

examples.scenario: It took Chiara four early shifts to admit the handoff lived in her head and nowhere near the bench. "When do I feed it?" the new baker asks, holding the starter jar beside a silent bench timer and an empty chart hook. Chiara has to decide whether to keep supervising or label the jar, post the feeding chart, and let the routine travel without her.
examples.whatToDo: Label the jar, set the bench timer beside the chart, and make the feeding sequence visible. Let the handoff guide the work.
examples.whyItMatters: Chiara should not be the fuel for every shift. The chart changes the path so the starter routine can continue without consuming her attention.

questions.prompt: A tutoring center has students waiting while one coordinator manually matches every request. What action best fits the catalyst model?
choices: Create a visible roster that routes common questions to peer tutors.
Tell students that waiting is part of learning.
Ask the coordinator to work through lunch.
questions.explanation: The roster changes the pathway from request to help. Longer hours add fuel from the coordinator, while the catalyst lets existing tutor energy move faster.

questions.prompt: A build pipeline wastes twenty minutes rebuilding the same packages before every deploy. Which choice changes the reaction pathway?
choices: Ask developers to wait more patiently.
Install a cache so completed work is reused before deployment.
Schedule deployments later in the evening.
questions.explanation: A cache accelerates progress by avoiding a repeated route. Patience and scheduling leave the wasteful pathway unchanged.

questions.prompt: A hospital intake desk delays families because nurses call one general line for every interpreter request. What would act most like a catalyst?
choices: A poster thanking nurses for trying hard.
A longer intake form with more patient history.
A language roster attached to intake that routes each request to the right interpreter.
questions.explanation: The roster changes the access path without being consumed by one case. The poster adds morale, and the longer form may increase drag.

questions.prompt: A repair cafe has enough volunteers, but appliances sit idle because nobody knows which bench or tool comes next. Which fix is catalytic?
choices: Add repair tickets that send each item to the right bench and tool bin.
Ask volunteers to look busier when guests arrive.
Ban complicated appliances from the queue.
questions.explanation: The ticket speeds the process by routing work. It does not repair the appliance itself, which is why it fits the catalyst move.

questions.prompt: A conference liaison answers the same prep questions all day: travel note, greenroom time, AV check, slide upload. What is the best catalyst candidate?
choices: A louder announcement that speakers should read emails.
A speaker brief organized in the order presenters need the details.
A second liaison who gives the same answers by hand.
questions.explanation: The brief changes the pathway for every presenter. A second liaison adds fuel, while the brief accelerates cleaner preparation without one-off rescue.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner personally reminds every new baker when to feed the starter. The jar, chart, and bench timer are never in one place. What is the strongest diagnosis?
choices: The owner is acting as fuel rather than creating a pathway changer.
The starter routine is impossible for new bakers.
The bakery should stop training people on early shifts.
questions.explanation: The owner is being consumed by repeated reminders. A labeled jar and chart would change the pathway so the routine moves without constant personal push.

questions.prompt: A manager calls a popular teammate a catalyst because everyone likes him, but every task still waits for him to push it personally. What is wrong with that label?
choices: A catalyst must change the process path, not merely supply effort each time.
A catalyst has to be a software tool, not a person.
A catalyst should make work slower so quality improves.
questions.explanation: The teammate may be useful, but if he is consumed by pushing every task, he is fuel. The model requires a pathway change.

questions.prompt: A customer support queue gets faster after a triage form sends billing, login, and refund requests to separate specialists. How should you evaluate the form?
choices: It is only administrative overhead because it does not answer tickets itself.
It may be catalytic because it changes the route and improves reaction rate.
It proves fewer specialists are needed no matter what demand looks like.
questions.explanation: The form is valuable because it changes the path work takes. It need not answer tickets to accelerate cleaner progress.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood tool library has drills available, but borrowers wait because staff manually explain the same safety steps. Which response transfers the catalyst model?
choices: Ask staff to speak faster during checkout.
Reduce the number of tools available.
Create a checkout card that routes borrowers through the safety steps before staff approval.
questions.explanation: The checkout card changes the pathway into approval. Faster talking adds staff fuel, while the card helps each borrower arrive prepared.

reviewCards.front: A process is slow even though people are working. What catalyst question should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Ask what would change the pathway so existing energy moves faster, cleaner, and with less repeated waste.

reviewCards.front: Someone helps every task by pushing personally. Why might that fail the catalyst test?
reviewCards.back: If the helper is consumed by each task, they are fuel. A catalyst changes the route so progress accelerates without constant rescue.

reviewCards.front: A roster, cache, or template speeds many handoffs. What feature makes it catalytic?
reviewCards.back: It changes how work travels. The accelerator stays useful across cases rather than becoming the energy source itself.

reviewCards.front: A team wants to add more labor to a slow pathway. What should be checked first?
reviewCards.back: Check whether the pathway itself is wasting effort. A catalyst may improve reaction rate before extra fuel is needed.

reviewCards.front: Why is faster progress not automatically better?
reviewCards.back: A catalyst can accelerate the wrong work too. First decide whether the reaction deserves a cleaner, faster path.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish extra fuel from pathway change. The skill is finding an accelerator that improves reaction rate without becoming the work itself.

ifThenPlans.plan: If people ask for more labor, then I will map the route work takes and look for one reusable pathway changer first.
If a pipeline repeats the same expensive step, then I will test a cache, template, or routing aid before adding capacity.
If one person answers the same question all day, then I will turn the answer into a brief or form that changes the next handoff.
If volunteers wait for direction, then I will add a visible ticket or roster that routes the next item to the right person.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one slow handoff today. Add a small reusable aid that changes the route for the next request without doing the work itself.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, identify one person or tool you call helpful. Ask whether it is fuel or a true catalyst, then redesign one pathway accordingly.

memorableLines.text: A true catalyst changes the way progress travels.
memorableLines.why: It draws the line between generic help and pathway change.

memorableLines.text: The accelerator is not the hero. The pathway is.
memorableLines.why: It keeps attention on route design rather than savior figures.

memorableLines.text: The room had energy. It lacked a pathway.
memorableLines.why: It makes the catalyst problem visible in a concrete scene.
